data.title: Insufficient Logging and Monitoring
data.summary:
Activity conducted throughout this assessment produced no detectable response,
indicating that logging and monitoring were insufficient to identify an attack in
progress.
data.description:
The assessment was conducted without any attempt to evade detection. Network
enumeration, credential attacks, lateral movement, and privilege escalation were
performed using standard tooling and default configurations, over a period of
several days.

At no point was any activity queried, blocked, or escalated. No contact was made
with the testing team regarding the traffic observed, and no account used during
the assessment was disabled or investigated.

Several categories of activity conducted would ordinarily generate events
suitable for detection, including authentication failures across multiple
accounts, requests for Kerberos service tickets using legacy encryption,
administrative authentication from unusual sources, and access to directory
objects associated with privilege escalation. The absence of any response
indicates either that these events are not being collected, that they are
collected but not analysed, or that alerting exists but does not reach a party
able to act on it.

Detection capability is a distinct control from prevention. The weaknesses
documented elsewhere in this report describe how an attacker gains access; this
finding describes why that access would continue undetected.
data.impact:
An attacker operating within the environment would be unlikely to be detected,
allowing the time between initial compromise and discovery to extend
indefinitely. This period determines the extent of the damage that can be caused,
as it governs how much data can be removed, how many systems can be reached, and
how thoroughly persistence can be established before any response begins.
Insufficient logging additionally impairs investigation after the event, as the
records required to establish what occurred are not available.
data.recommendation:
1. Collect security event logs centrally from all domain controllers, servers,
   workstations, and network infrastructure, retaining them for a period
   sufficient to support investigation of an intrusion discovered late.

2. Forward logs to a system outside the monitored environment, so that an
   attacker holding administrative access to a host cannot alter the record of
   their activity.

3. Implement detection rules for the activity classes identified during this
   assessment, including authentication failures aggregated across accounts,
   Kerberos ticket requests using legacy encryption, and modification of
   privileged group membership and directory object permissions.

4. Deploy endpoint detection capable of identifying credential access and
   suspicious process behaviour, which produces signals unavailable from
   operating system logs alone.

5. Define and document a response process specifying who receives alerts, within
   what timeframe they are triaged, and what authority they hold to act.

6. Validate detection capability periodically through structured testing, so that
   coverage gaps are identified deliberately rather than during an incident.
